summary: Defines a Telnet authentication mechanism using the Digital Signature Algorithm. It builds on the Telnet Authentication Option.

eli5.summary: This lets Telnet use digital signatures, a kind of unforgeable handwriting, to prove who is connecting.

questions: how does telnet authentication using dsa work
what is dss authentication type in telnet
does telnet dsa provide session integrity
what is the difference between one-way and mutual telnet authentication
subtitle: How a Telnet client proves who it is, and optionally checks the server, using DSA digital signatures and certificates.

tldr.problem: Telnet has no concept of security. Its usual login sends a user name and password in the clear, and the server never proves its own identity to the user.
tldr.mechanism: Within the Telnet Authentication Option (RFC 2941), the client and server swap signed tokens and X.509 certificates holding DSS public keys, following NIST FIPS PUB 196, to authenticate the client or both sides.
tldr.outcome: It gives authentication only. The RFC says it does not provide session integrity, so it is a way to prove identity at login rather than to protect the whole session.

today: RFC 2943 is a Proposed Standard from September 2000. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Telnet Needs an Authentication Mechanism
sections.content:
TELNET on its own has no concept of security. Without negotiated options it just passes characters between the two network virtual terminals. In its most common use, remote terminal access on TCP port 23, the server asks for a user name and password in the clear, and the server does not authenticate itself to the user.

The TELNET Authentication Option (RFC 2941) adds user authentication and server authentication. The two sides first agree to support the option. Then the server offers a preference-ordered list of authentication types, each with a modifier saying whether the authentication is one-way or mutual and in which direction. The client picks one and replies with the first set of authentication data. They then run as many exchanges as the chosen type needs.

RFC 2943 defines one such type, built on the Digital Signature Algorithm.
sections.eli5: Plain Telnet is like shouting your password across a crowded room. The authentication option lets the two computers agree on a safer way to show who they are.

sections.title: Using DSA with the Authentication Option
sections.content:
The Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA), also called the Digital Signature Standard (DSS), is used with SHA-1. The RFC uses the two names interchangeably. DSA can give unilateral or mutual authentication.

The specification follows the tokens and exchanges of NIST FIPS PUB 196, which defines entity authentication with public key cryptography, including the ASN.1 encoding of messages and tokens. The RFC picks a conformant subset of the fields and subfields.

Because Telnet works character by character, it is not well suited to integrity-only services. This profile therefore provides authentication but not session integrity.

All data covered by a digital signature MUST be encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). Other data may use either BER or DER.
sections.eli5: A digital signature is like a stamp only you own. The RFC says how to use the stamp to prove who you are when you log in, but it does not promise nobody can tamper with what you type afterwards.

sections.title: One-Way Authentication of the Client
sections.content:
Unilateral authentication must be done client-to-server. The client is Party A and the server is Party B. After the usual IAC DO/WILL AUTHENTICATION exchange and the server's SEND list, the client may send its user name with the NAME sub-option. The name must be sent after the server's list and before the client finishes the exchange, which stops the server from prompting for a name and password in the clear.

The two-octet authentication type pair for one-way DSS is DSS AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER | AUTH_HOW_ONE_WAY | ENCRYPT_OFF | INI_CRED_FWD_OFF. It means the client is authenticated to the server and no encryption is done. A single octet sub-option identifier follows the pair so each step of the open-ended exchange is easy to recognise.

  • The client sends DSS_INITIALIZE.
  • The server replies with DSS_TOKENBA, carrying TokenBA.
  • The client sends DSS_CERTA_TOKENAB, carrying its certificate CertA and TokenAB.

Both certificates are X.509 certificates that contain DSS public keys. The client must validate the server's certificate before using the DSA public key in it. At the end, the client is authenticated to the server.
sections.eli5: The client says hello, the server hands over a fresh challenge, and the client signs it and sends back its ID card. The server checks the signature and knows who it is talking to.

sections.title: Mutual Authentication
sections.content:
Mutual authentication is slightly more complex. The type pair is DSS AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER | AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL | ENCRYPT_OFF | INI_CRED_FWD_OFF, meaning the client and server authenticate each other and no encryption is done.

The first three steps match the one-way case: DSS_INITIALIZE, DSS_TOKENBA and DSS_CERTA_TOKENAB. The mutual case adds a final server message, DSS_CERTB_TOKENBA2, which carries the server's certificate CertB and a second signed token, TokenBA2. That last step is what lets the client check the server.
sections.eli5: For mutual checking, the server also signs something and shows its own ID card at the end, so both sides know who the other is.

sections.title: ASN.1 Messages and Token Types
sections.content:
The RFC gives the ASN.1 syntax for its subset of FIPS 196 and includes no optional fields or subfields. The structures are MessageBA (TokenBA), MessageAB (CertA and TokenAB) and MessageBA2 (CertB and TokenBA2).

Each token holds random numbers and a timestamp. A RandomNumber is an integer of 20 octets. TokenAB and TokenBA2 also carry the name of the other party and a signature value. All DSA signature values are encoded as a sequence of two integers, following RFC 2459, section 7.2.2.

Every message starts with a TokenId holding a tokenType and a protocol version number that is always 0x0001. The token type tells the receiver which message it is and whether the run is unilateral or mutual.
sections.eli5: Each message is a form with fixed boxes: a random number, the time, and a signature. The first box says which kind of form it is.

sections.title: Protecting Keys and Random Values
sections.content:
The whole memo is about security mechanisms. For DSA to authenticate anyone, the implementation must protect the private key from disclosure.

Implementations must generate DSS private keys, the k values used in DSS signatures, and nonces randomly. A weak pseudo-random number generator can leave little or no security, because an attacker may reproduce its environment and search the small set of possible values instead of brute-forcing. The RFC points to RFC 1750 and to Appendix 3 of FIPS PUB 186 for guidance.
sections.eli5: Keep your stamp safe, and pick your secret numbers by really rolling the dice. If your dice are rigged, a sneaky person can guess your numbers.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The authentication type DSS and its sub-option values are registered with IANA. Any sub-option values used to extend the protocol must be registered before use, and IANA is told not to issue new sub-option values without documentation of their use.

The RFC lists the codes it uses. The option AUTHENTICATION is 37, the type DSS is 14, and the sub-option commands are 1 to 4.
sections.eli5: The numbers used for each kind of message are written in an official list, so everyone uses the same numbers for the same things.
